newsitem.title: INDIA: Gujral's allies hail India insurance law withdrawl.
newsitem.headline: Gujral's allies hail India insurance law withdrawl.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's leftwing allies, opposed to allowing private firms into the insurance sector, on Wednesday welcomed his decision to withdraw a bill to set up an insurance regulator.
The government failed to win enough support in the lower house of parliament to defeat an opposition-backed amendment barring foreign multinationals from the insurance sector.
The Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPM) said its politburo "welcomes the government's decision to withdraw the Insurance Regulatory Authority Bill in the face of stiff opposition".

The bill would have created an insurance watchdog agency to oversee the state-controlled industry, and was considered an important first step towards the eventual opening up of the sector to private competition, both Indian and foreign.

Earlier on Wednesday, the lower house rejected an amendment proposed by the CPM, which is part of Gujral's coalition, to bar private firms from the insurance sector. The amendment was defeated by a 228-to-43 vote in the 545-seat house.
It was the first time since Gujral's coalition government assumed office last year after inconclusive general elections that his leftwing allies voted against the government.
But the amendment to block the entry of foreign firms, sponsored by the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party, attracted enough support to force Gujral to retract the bill.

"For over many months the Left, democratic, patriotic forces and the working class of the country have been opposing the move to privatise the insurance sector as this would be detrimental to India's self reliance," the CPM said.
India began opening up its economy in 1991 by dismantling decades-old socialist controls on trade and industry.
But the insurance sector remains state-controlled, and is closed to private firms, both foreign and domestic.
India's foreign allies, led by the United States, have pressed it to liberalise its insurance sector, saying the move would improve service and boost domestic savings.
Finance Minister P. Chidamabaram, a free trader in Gujral's disparate coalition, has often expressed his commitment to further liberalise the economy.
"It is victory for the trade unions and those supporting public sector units against Chidambaram's economic policies," said Communist Party of India leader Gurudas Dasgupta.
